title: Demand management: monetary and fiscal policy
summary: Central banks use interest rates, open market operations, reserve requirements and quantitative easing; governments use taxes and spending. Both shift AD but face time lags and constraints. HL covers money creation and the Keynesian multiplier.

keyterms.definition: Central bank action on interest rates and the money supply to influence AD, usually to meet an inflation target.
The institution that issues currency, sets the policy interest rate, acts as banker to the government and lender of last resort.
The rate the central bank charges commercial banks, which influences all other interest rates in the economy.
Central bank buying or selling government bonds to change the money supply and interest rates.
The share of deposits commercial banks must hold in reserve; raising it reduces banks’ ability to lend.
Large-scale central bank purchases of bonds and other assets to lower long-term interest rates when policy rates are near zero.
The nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate.
The use of government spending and taxation to influence AD.
When government spending exceeds tax revenue in a year.
Taxes and transfers that change automatically with the cycle, e.g. unemployment benefits rise and tax revenue falls in a recession.
When government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment, weakening the effect of fiscal expansion.
Delays between recognising a problem, acting and the policy taking effect.
Commercial banks create new deposits (money) when they make loans, limited by reserves and demand for credit.
The ratio of the final change in real GDP to the initial change in spending: k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ (MPS + MPT + MPM).
The share of an extra unit of income that is spent on domestic consumption.

questions.prompt: To reduce high inflation, a central bank is most likely to…
questions.explanation: Higher interest rates reduce borrowing and spending, so AD falls.

questions.prompt: Order the transmission of an interest rate cut.
items: Central bank cuts the policy rate
Borrowing for consumption and investment rises
questions.explanation: Lower rates reduce the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving.

questions.statement: When a central bank sells government bonds, the money supply tends to fall.
questions.explanation: Buyers pay the central bank, draining reserves from the banking system.

questions.text: Nominal interest rate 5%, inflation 3%. The real interest rate is ___%.
questions.explanation: Real rate ≈ nominal − inflation = 2%.

questions.prompt: Why did central banks use quantitative easing after 2008 and in 2020?
options: Policy rates were already close to zero
questions.explanation: QE buys assets to lower long-term rates when the policy rate cannot fall further.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to its expansionary use.
questions.explanation: Each increases money supply or lowers interest rates to raise AD.

questions.prompt: Which is a constraint on expansionary monetary policy in a deep recession?
options: Low confidence means people may not borrow even at low rates
questions.explanation: Low confidence and the zero lower bound limit monetary policy ("pushing on a string").

questions.statement: An advantage of monetary policy is that independent central banks can change rates quickly, free of political pressure.
questions.explanation: Decisions can be made at regular meetings without legislation.

questions.text: Central bank buying or selling of government bonds is called ___ market operations.
questions.explanation: OMOs are a routine way to manage liquidity and interest rates.

questions.prompt: Higher interest rates can also reduce AD through the exchange rate because…
options: hot money inflows raise the currency’s value, making exports dearer
questions.explanation: An appreciation reduces net exports.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of expansionary fiscal policy?
options: Cutting income tax and raising infrastructure spending
questions.explanation: Lower taxes and higher spending raise AD.

questions.statement: Unemployment benefits act as an automatic stabiliser.
questions.explanation: They rise automatically in a downturn, supporting incomes and AD without new decisions.

questions.text: Government spending greater than tax revenue in a year is a budget ___.
questions.explanation: Deficits add to government debt.

options: Government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment
questions.explanation: It reduces the net effect of fiscal expansion on AD.

questions.prompt: Match each item to its category.
questions.explanation: Government revenue and spending have several categories.

questions.prompt: Which is a key weakness of discretionary fiscal policy?
options: Long time lags in planning and approving spending
questions.explanation: By the time spending happens, the economy may already be recovering.

questions.statement: Fiscal policy can target specific regions or industries more easily than monetary policy.
questions.explanation: Spending and tax changes can be directed, whereas interest rates affect everyone.

questions.prompt: In a recession with very low interest rates, why might fiscal policy be preferred?
options: Fiscal policy has no time lags
Monetary policy has little room left, and government spending directly raises AD
questions.explanation: At the zero lower bound, fiscal stimulus is often more powerful.

questions.text: Delays between identifying a problem and a policy having an effect are time ___.
questions.explanation: Both monetary and fiscal policy suffer lags.

questions.prompt: Order the effect of a fiscal stimulus.
items: AD and real GDP rise by more than the initial spending
questions.explanation: The extra rounds of spending are the multiplier effect.

lessons.title: HL: Money creation and the multiplier

questions.prompt: MPS = 0.1, MPT = 0.2, MPM = 0.2. What is the multiplier?

questions.text: With a multiplier of 2, a $5 bn rise in government spending raises real GDP by $___ bn.

questions.prompt: If MPC (domestic) is 0.75, the multiplier is…

questions.statement: A higher marginal propensity to import makes the multiplier smaller.
questions.explanation: More of each extra dollar leaks abroad rather than being re-spent domestically.

questions.prompt: Government wants real GDP to rise by $12 bn. The multiplier is 3. What initial injection is needed?

questions.statement: Commercial banks create money when they make loans.
questions.explanation: A loan creates a new deposit in the borrower’s account.

questions.prompt: How does a higher minimum reserve requirement affect money creation?
options: Banks can lend less from each deposit, so less money is created
questions.explanation: More must be held in reserve, reducing lending.

questions.text: The share of extra income spent on domestic consumption is the marginal propensity to ___.
questions.explanation: MPC + MPS + MPT + MPM = 1.

questions.prompt: Match each leakage to its propensity.
questions.explanation: The multiplier = 1 ÷ (sum of marginal propensities to withdraw).

questions.prompt: Order the multiplier process after $100 m of new investment (MPC = 0.5).
items: $100 m becomes income for workers and firms
$50 m is spent on domestic output
$25 m is spent in the next round
Total rise in GDP approaches $200 m
questions.explanation: Each round is half the previous one; k = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.
